claims.text: A hybrid ab initio phonon-transport and machine-learning approach can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The approach will predict the separate transport contributions to within ±10% of measurements from 50 to 1200 K.
The ±10% accuracy will apply to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
The new approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 30% relative to prior empirical or purely DFT methods.
Arc melting and annealing will produce equimolar HfNbTaTiZr with 0.2–1 wt.% oxygen and a uniform microstructure.
Large-scale ab initio calculations can represent both chemical disorder and oxygen-impurity scattering for training the machine-learning workflow.
An inert measurement atmosphere will minimize additional oxidation or contamination between 50 and 1200 K.
Oxygen impurities act as scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Multi-principal-element disorder independently affects phonon and electronic transport channels.
Separate phonon and electron submodels avoid the oversimplifications of Debye-type or purely DFT-based approaches.
The hybrid framework better captures scattering interactions caused by atomic-mass and force-constant fluctuations.
For both pristine and oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr, predicted total and channel-specific conductivities will deviate by no more than ±10% from experiment over 50–1200 K.
Previous simplified models exhibit deviations of up to 30% in total conductivity for pristine and oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr.
Debye-based and pure first-principles methods often fail to match separate lattice and electronic conductivity measurements across 50–1200 K.
The model is applicable to near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Compositions substantially different from near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr or oxygen contents above 1 wt.% may require model retraining.
Microstructural variation, unaccounted phases, and unmodeled scattering mechanisms may reduce predictive accuracy.
A deviation greater than ±10% in either measured lattice or electronic conductivity at investigated temperatures and oxygen levels falsifies the hypothesis.
